title: The Zahiris
hook: the literalist school of Ibn Hazm, now small

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ibadis of Oman: a school with its own name, asking to be called by it.

A sign on a park gate says: no dogs. Someone walks in with a pet wolf. Is that allowed? One kind of reader reaches for the purpose behind the sign and says no, obviously. Another kind stops and asks: who decides what the sign meant beyond what it says? If the rule-maker wanted wolves kept out, couldn't the rule-maker have written it? That second reader isn't being silly. That reader is protecting the text from everyone's guesses. In Islamic law, that reader had a school, and its great voice lived in Muslim Spain. Today, the Zahiris.
screen: `NO DOGS. IN COMES A WOLF.` → `THE PURPOSE, OR THE WORDS?` → `A SCHOOL OF THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Zahir is Arabic for what's outward, what shows on the surface. The Zahiris are the people of the plain sense: the law is what the Qur'an and the sunnah actually say, read in their apparent meaning. Tradition names Dawud al-Zahiri of Baghdad as the founder. Next, the tool they put down. Other schools use qiyas, analogy: if wine is forbidden because it intoxicates, so is any drink that intoxicates. The Zahiris refused analogy as a source of law. Where the texts speak, follow them. Where they're silent, the matter is left open, and no jurist may close it with a guess. Then their great voice. Ibn Hazm of Cordoba wrote the method out at full length, in a book of law called al-Muhalla, arguing case by case. Tradition remembers him as sharp-tongued and fearless in debate, and he also wrote a book about love, The Ring of the Dove, full of lovers, glances and letters. Last, a test case. The Qur'an tells children, about aging parents, in Pickthall's words, "say not 'Fie' unto them nor repulse them, but speak unto them a gracious word." An analogist says: if even 'fie' is forbidden, striking a parent is forbidden all the more. A Zahiri agrees on the result, not the route. The same verses already command kindness, and other texts forbid harm. The plain sense is enough. The school is small today, but its question still sits in classrooms of fiqh: are you reading the text, or reading yourself into it?
screen: `ZAHIR: WHAT SHOWS ON THE SURFACE.` · `NO ANALOGY. SILENCE STAYS OPEN.` · `IBN HAZM OF CORDOBA.` · `NOT EVEN 'FIE.'`

segments.voice: Take one short message you got recently, a text, an email, a note on the fridge, and read it once exactly as written, nothing added. Then read it again with everything you know about the person who sent it, and notice the gap between the two readings, and how much of the second one you supplied yourself. If you pray, you can ask to read well.
The Zahiris. The school of the plain sense: the law is what the texts outwardly say, with no analogy to fill their silences. Today's word.
Your line: the plain sense. The words come first, and the guessing after. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Zahiri jurists derive law only from the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and sunnah, rejecting analogy (qiyas); the school is small today, but Ibn Hazm's books are still read by students of law.

what it means: the Zahiris read the plain sense on purpose, to keep jurists' guesses from becoming law.

chat.says: Why would a whole school of law refuse to use analogy?
options: To guard the text: where it's silent, the matter stays open, not filled by a guess.
Because they thought the Qur'an and the sunnah didn't settle much of anything.
Because analogy hadn't been thought of yet when their school began.
